meta.titre: Ecosystems and Energy Flow: trophic levels, losses and productivity
meta.sous_theme: Feeding groups, energy transfer between trophic levels and net primary productivity

sections.contenu_markdown: A maize field in the Western Highlands, a stretch of savanna in the north of Cameroon and a patch of forest in the south all work as ecosystems. In each one, sunlight grows plants, animals eat the plants or each other, and bacteria and fungi break down whatever dies. The energy that grows a blade of grass is the same energy that finally warms the air as a lion rests. Examiners like this theme because it asks you to name feeding groups exactly and to explain why chains are short and why top carnivores are few. Master the vocabulary and the simple energy arithmetic and you collect easy marks.

items: Green plants make food by photosynthesis, using light energy, carbon dioxide and water.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only changed from one form to another.
Respiration releases energy from food, and part of that energy is lost as heat.
A percentage is a part divided by the whole, multiplied by 100.

sections.titre: Trophic levels, energy transfer and productivity
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Components of an ecosystem
An ecosystem is a community of living things (biotic) interacting with the non-living environment (abiotic: light, water, soil, temperature). Energy enters as sunlight and is captured by producers.

| Group | Obtains food by | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Producer (autotroph) | photosynthesis | grass, trees, phytoplankton |
| Primary consumer (herbivore) | eating producers | grasshopper, antelope |
| Secondary consumer (carnivore) | eating primary consumers | frog, lion hunting antelope |
| Tertiary consumer | eating secondary consumers | hawk eating a snake |
| Omnivore | eating both plants and animals | humans, pigs, chickens |
| Decomposer | breaking down dead matter and returning nutrients | bacteria, fungi |
| Detritivore | feeding on fragments of dead matter | earthworm, woodlouse |

### Trophic levels and energy transfer
A **trophic level** is a feeding position in a food chain. In a chain the arrow points from the food to the feeder, showing the direction of energy flow. Only a fraction of the energy at one level reaches the next. Some parts are never eaten (roots, bones), some are not digested and are lost in faeces, and much is lost as heat in respiration, movement and body maintenance. As a rough guide about 10% passes up each level, although real values vary between ecosystems. For this reason chains rarely have more than four or five links and top carnivores are few.

**Energy flows in one direction** (sun to producers to consumers, ending as heat); **nutrients cycle** between living things and stores in biomass, litter and soil.

### Pyramids
Pyramids of numbers can have odd shapes (one large tree supports thousands of insects). Pyramids of biomass can be inverted in the sea, where fast-growing phytoplankton are eaten almost as quickly as they reproduce. A pyramid of energy (per unit area per year) is always upright.

### Productivity
Gross primary productivity (GPP) is the total energy fixed by photosynthesis. Net primary productivity (NPP) is what remains after the plants' own respiration (R):

$$NPP = GPP - R$$

NPP is the energy available to consumers. It is high in warm, wet environments with a long growing season such as the tropical rainforest, and low in deserts and cold tundra.
sections.formule_principale: $$\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{energy at the higher level}}{\text{energy at the lower level}} \times 100$$

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to describe feeding relationships or the effect of removing a species.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A food chain shows one path of energy. A food web joins many chains, because most animals eat more than one kind of food. If one species is removed, others that fed on it may starve, while the species it fed on may increase, so a web is more stable than a single chain.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives energy values per square metre per year.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use the same units throughout. Find NPP by subtracting respiration from GPP, then find the transfer efficiency between neighbouring levels by dividing the higher by the lower and multiplying by 100. Explain the loss as heat, undigested matter and uneaten parts, not as energy being destroyed.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question compares ecosystems such as tropical rainforest and cold forest.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Nutrients are held in three stores: biomass, litter and soil. In the tropical rainforest the biomass store is large, the litter store is small because decomposition is fast in heat and moisture, and the soil store is small because heavy rain leaches nutrients away. In cold forests decomposition is slow, so the litter store is larger.

sections.enonce_markdown:
A pond ecosystem fixes 10,000 kJ per square metre per year by photosynthesis. The plants lose 4,000 kJ per square metre per year in respiration. Water insects (primary consumers) store 600 kJ per square metre per year and small fish (secondary consumers) store 72 kJ per square metre per year.

(a) Calculate the NPP.
(b) Calculate the percentage of energy passed from the producers (NPP) to the insects, and from the insects to the fish.
(c) Explain why less energy is available at each higher level. (9 marks)

etapes.justification: NPP is the energy left after the plants have used part of what they fixed.
Efficiency compares the energy that arrives at the higher level with the energy that was available at the lower one.
The same method is used between the next pair of levels.

etapes.action: Find how much energy is lost between the producers and the fish.
etapes.justification: This shows how little of the original NPP reaches the top of the chain.

etapes.action: Give the reasons for the losses.
etapes.justification: The question says explain, so each loss must be named and linked to a process.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Heat is released in respiration by every organism; parts such as roots, shells and bones are not eaten; some food is not digested and is lost in faeces; some energy is used for movement and keeping warm. Energy is not destroyed: it leaves the food chain as heat.

sections.conclusion_markdown: NPP is **6,000 kJ per square metre per year**. The transfer efficiencies are **10%** (producers to insects) and **12%** (insects to fish). About **98.8%** of the NPP is lost before it reaches the small fish, mainly as heat, and that is why food chains are short. At about 10% a third consumer would receive only 7.2 kJ per square metre per year.

items.erreur_markdown: "Humans are carnivores because they eat meat."
items.pourquoi_faux: A carnivore eats only animals. Humans normally eat both plant and animal food, so they are omnivores.
items.correction_markdown: Define omnivores as animals that feed on both plants and animals, and carnivores as animals that feed on other animals only.

items.pourquoi_faux: Energy flows one way and leaves as heat. It is nutrients (carbon, nitrogen and so on) that are recycled.
items.correction_markdown: Write that energy flows through the ecosystem, while nutrients cycle between living things and the stores in soil, litter and biomass.

items.erreur_markdown: A food chain drawn as grass <- grasshopper <- frog, with arrows pointing from the feeder to the food.
items.pourquoi_faux: Arrows show the direction in which energy passes, from the food to the one that eats it.
items.correction_markdown: Draw grass -> grasshopper -> frog, and label the producer and the consumers.

items.erreur_markdown: "The 90% that is not passed on is destroyed."
items.pourquoi_faux: Energy cannot be destroyed. Most of it is released as heat in respiration or remains in uneaten and undigested material.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the energy is lost from the food chain as heat or passed to decomposers, not destroyed.

items.erreur_markdown: Leaving decomposers out of an ecosystem description.
items.pourquoi_faux: Without bacteria and fungi, dead matter would not be broken down and nutrients would not return to the soil for producers to use.
items.correction_markdown: Include decomposers as the group that recycles nutrients, and say that they release energy as heat when they respire.

items.enonce_markdown: Name the feeding group of each organism: (a) grass; (b) a grasshopper eating grass; (c) a frog eating grasshoppers; (d) a snake eating frogs; (e) a fungus on a dead log; (f) a person who eats rice and fish. Then write the food chain linking (a) to (d) using arrows.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **producer**; (b) **primary consumer (herbivore)**; (c) **secondary consumer (carnivore)**; (d) **tertiary consumer**; (e) **decomposer**; (f) **omnivore**, because the person eats a plant food and an animal food.

Food chain: grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake.

items.enonce_markdown: In a forest the GPP is 15,000 kJ per square metre per year and the plants respire 9,000 kJ per square metre per year. Assume 10% of the energy passes to each higher trophic level. (a) Calculate the NPP. (b) Calculate the energy at the second, third and fourth trophic levels. (c) Explain why a fifth level is unlikely to support many animals.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $NPP = 15\,000 - 9\,000 = $ **6,000 kJ m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$**.
(b) Second level: $6\,000 \times 0.10 = $ **600**; third level: $600 \times 0.10 = $ **60**; fourth level: $60 \times 0.10 = $ **6** kJ m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$.
(c) The fourth level receives only $\frac{6}{6\,000} \times 100 = 0.1\%$ of the NPP. A fifth level would receive about 0.6 kJ m$^{-2}$ yr$^{-1}$, too little to feed more than a few individuals, because energy is lost as heat, in faeces and in uneaten parts at every transfer.

items.enonce_markdown: In a lake, phytoplankton have a standing biomass of 5 g per square metre and zooplankton have 12 g per square metre. Their productivities are 800 and 80 kJ per square metre per year respectively. (a) State the shape of each pyramid (biomass and energy). (b) Explain how the biomass pyramid can have this shape. (c) Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer and say why the energy pyramid cannot be inverted.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The biomass pyramid is **inverted** (5 g below 12 g); the energy pyramid is **upright** (800 above 80).
(b) Phytoplankton reproduce very quickly and are eaten almost as fast as they grow, so a small standing crop at any moment can support a larger biomass of zooplankton over time. Biomass is a snapshot, while productivity is a rate.
(c) $\frac{80}{800} \times 100 = $ **10%**. Energy is lost at each transfer as heat, so the energy available at a higher level over a year is always smaller than at the level below, and the energy pyramid cannot be inverted.

items_markdown: Producers capture light energy; consumers are primary (herbivores), secondary or tertiary (carnivores), or omnivores (plants and animals); decomposers and detritivores break down dead matter and return nutrients.
Energy flows one way through trophic levels and leaves as heat, while nutrients are recycled.
Roughly 10% of the energy passes to the next level, the rest is lost as heat, undigested matter and uneaten parts, so chains are short and top carnivores are few.
Pyramids of energy are always upright; pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted.
NPP = GPP minus plant respiration; it is highest in warm, wet environments such as the tropical rainforest.
In calculations use the same units, show the formula and the substitution, and explain losses as heat rather than destroyed energy.
